title: UNIT 4: ENERGY CHANGES AND ELECTROCHEMISTRY
notes: Chemical reactions involve energy changes, while electrochemistry deals with the conversion between chemical and electrical energy.

title: 4.1 Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
notes:
Chemical reactions involve changes in energy because the energy of reactants differs from that of products. Chemical energy is a form of potential energy stored in chemical bonds and intermolecular forces.

◆ UNIVERSE
✓ System → Part being studied.
✓ Surroundings → Everything outside the system.

✓ Internal energy → The sum of potential and kinetic energies.

ΔE = Efinal − Einitial

✓ Energy can be transferred between a system and its surroundings as heat or work:
ΔE = q + w.

title: 4.1.1 Exothermic Reactions
notes:
✓ An exothermic reaction → A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings, causing the surroundings to become warmer.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Combustion of fuels.
✓ Burning carbon in oxygen.
✓ Dissolving NaOH in water.

✓ For an exothermic reaction:
ΔH < 0

→ The products have lower enthalpy than the reactants.

title: 4.1.2 Endothermic Reactions
notes:
✓ An endothermic reaction → A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings, causing the surroundings to become cooler.

◆ EXAMPLE
Dissolving KNO₃ in water absorbs heat and lowers the temperature.

✓ For an endothermic reaction:
ΔH > 0

→ The products have higher enthalpy than the reactants.

title: 4.1.3 Enthalpy Change
notes:
✓ Enthalpy change → The heat change of a reaction at constant temperature and pressure.

ΔH = Hproducts − Hreactants

✓ Exothermic:
ΔH < 0 → Heat released.

✓ Endothermic:
ΔH > 0 → Heat absorbed.

✓ Energy-level diagrams → Show the relative enthalpy of reactants and products.

title: 4.1.4 Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity
notes:
✓ A calorimeter → An instrument used to measure heat released or absorbed during a reaction.

✓ Heat capacity → The quantity of heat required to change the temperature of an object by 1 K.

Heat capacity = q/ΔT

✓ Specific heat capacity → The heat required to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 K.

c = q/(mΔT)

Therefore:
q = mcΔT

✓ Unit of heat capacity → J/K.

title: 4.2 Energy Changes in Electrochemistry
notes:
✓ Electrochemistry → The study of the interconversion of chemical and electrical energy.

◆ It involves:
✓ Using electricity to cause chemical reactions.
✓ Generating electricity from chemical reactions.

→ Chemical energy ⇌ Electrical energy.

title: 4.2.1 Electrical Conductivity
notes:
✓ Electrical conductivity → The ability of a substance to transmit electricity. Electric current is carried by charged particles.

◆ CHARGE CARRIERS
✓ Electrons → Negative charge.
✓ Cations → Positive charge.
✓ Anions → Negative charge.

◆ TYPES OF ELECTRICAL CONDUCTIVITY
✓ Metallic conductivity.
✓ Electrolytic conductivity.

title: 4.2.2 Metallic Conductivity
notes:
✓ Metallic conductivity → Conductivity that occurs because freely moving electrons carry electric charge through metals.

◆ EXAMPLES
Copper, iron and magnesium are good metallic conductors.

◆ METALLIC CONDUCTION
✓ Charge carriers → Electrons.
✓ No transfer of matter occurs.
✓ No chemical decomposition normally occurs.
✓ Resistance is affected by temperature and movement of metal atoms.

title: 4.2.3 Electrolytic Conductivity
notes:
✓ Electrolytic conductivity → Conductivity that occurs when ions move through an electrolyte in aqueous solution or in the molten state.

✓ Electrolytes contain mobile ions that carry electric current.

◆ EXAMPLE
NaCl(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

✓ Electrolytic conduction → Involves movement of matter as ions and may cause chemical changes at the electrodes.

title: 4.2.4 Metallic vs Electrolytic Conductivity
notes:
◆ METALLIC CONDUCTIVITY
✓ Charge carriers → Electrons.
✓ Occurs mainly in metals.
✓ No transfer of matter.
✓ Normally no chemical decomposition.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC CONDUCTIVITY
✓ Charge carriers → Ions.
✓ Occurs in molten electrolytes or solutions.
✓ Involves transfer of matter as ions.
✓ Chemical changes can occur at electrodes.

◆ REMEMBER
→ Metal → Electrons.
→ Electrolyte → Ions.

title: 4.2.5 Electrolytes and Nonelectrolytes
notes:
✓ Electrolyte → A substance that produces mobile ions and conducts electricity when dissolved in water or in the molten state.

✓ Strong electrolyte → Completely dissociates into ions.
Example: NaCl.

✓ Weak electrolyte → Partially ionizes into ions.
Examples: CH₃COOH and HNO₂.

✓ Nonelectrolyte → A substance that does not produce ions and does not conduct electricity.
Example: Sugar, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.

title: 4.3 Voltaic (Galvanic) Cells
notes:
✓ A voltaic or galvanic cell → A cell that converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.

◆ DANIELL CELL

✓ Anode:
Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻

✓ Cathode:
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)

✓ Overall:
Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

→ Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc anode to the copper cathode.

title: 4.3.1 Salt Bridge
notes:
✓ A salt bridge → Connects the two half-cells of a Daniell or other suitable voltaic cell.

✓ Main function → Maintains electrical neutrality between the two solutions so that the cell can continue producing electricity.

→ Without charge balance, the redox reaction would stop.

title: 4.3.2 Types of Voltaic Cells
notes:
◆ THREE IMPORTANT TYPES
✓ Daniell cell → Uses Zn and Cu half-cells connected by a salt bridge.
✓ Leclanché cell → Zinc-carbon dry cell commonly used in portable devices such as flashlights and radios.
✓ Lead-storage cell → Secondary cell that can be recharged and is widely used in batteries.

✓ The Leclanché cell uses a zinc container as the anode and a graphite rod surrounded by manganese dioxide and electrolyte paste.

title: 4.3.3 Lead-Storage Battery
notes:
✓ A lead-storage battery → A rechargeable secondary cell.
✓ One cell produces about 2 V, so six cells connected in series produce about 12 V.

◆ DURING DISCHARGE
✓ Anode:
Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻

✓ Cathode:
PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

✓ Overall:
Pb + PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O

→ During charging, the reactions are reversed.

title: 4.4 Electrolysis
notes:
✓ Electrolysis → The use of electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

→ The word electrolysis means breakdown by electricity.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC CELL COMPONENTS
✓ Electrolyte.
✓ Anode.
✓ Cathode.
✓ External electrical source.

✓ At the cathode → Reduction occurs.
✓ At the anode → Oxidation occurs.

◆ MEMORY TIP
✓ AN OX → Anode Oxidation.
✓ RED CAT → Reduction Cathode.

title: 4.4.1 Electrolysis of Molten Electrolytes
notes:
✓ When an ionic solid is melted, its ions become free to move and can conduct electricity.

◆ EXAMPLE: MOLTEN NaCl

✓ Cathode:
Na⁺(l) + e⁻ → Na(l)

✓ Anode:
Cl⁻(l) → ½Cl₂(g) + e⁻

✓ Overall:
Na⁺(l) + Cl⁻(l) → Na(l) + ½Cl₂(g)

→ Electrolysis of molten salts is used to obtain highly reactive metals such as sodium, lithium, magnesium and calcium.

title: 4.4.2 Electrolytic Cell vs Voltaic Cell
notes:
◆ VOLTAIC CELL
✓ Chemical energy → Electrical energy.
✓ Spontaneous redox reaction.
✓ Produces electricity.
✓ Anode → Negative.
✓ Cathode → Positive.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC CELL
✓ Electrical energy → Chemical energy.
✓ Non-spontaneous reaction.
✓ Consumes electricity.
✓ Anode → Positive.
✓ Cathode → Negative.

◆ IMPORTANT
→ The signs of the electrodes change, but the reactions do not:
✓ Anode → Oxidation.
✓ Cathode → Reduction.

title: UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
◆ ENERGY
✓ ΔE = q + w
✓ ΔE = Efinal − Einitial

◆ ENTHALPY
✓ ΔH = Hproducts − Hreactants
✓ Exothermic → ΔH < 0 → Releases heat.
✓ Endothermic → ΔH > 0 → Absorbs heat.

◆ HEAT
✓ Heat capacity = q/ΔT
✓ c = q/(mΔT)
✓ q = mcΔT

◆ ELECTROCHEMISTRY
→ Chemical energy ⇌ Electrical energy.

◆ CONDUCTIVITY
→ Metal → Electrons.
→ Electrolyte → Ions.

◆ CELLS
✓ Anode → Oxidation.
✓ Cathode → Reduction.

◆ VOLTAIC
→ Chemical → Electrical.
✓ Anode = Negative.
✓ Cathode = Positive.

◆ ELECTROLYTIC
→ Electrical → Chemical.
✓ Anode = Positive.
✓ Cathode = Negative.

◆ EXAM TIP
✓ Never identify anode or cathode from its sign alone. First remember the universal rule:
Anode → Oxidation.
Cathode → Reduction.
